analysis.one_liner: Raises worker recovery in corporate bankruptcies and caps executive bonuses at failing companies.
analysis.headline: Six senators — five Democrats and one Republican — back the bill, but since its April 2025 referral it has received no committee hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, current law puts much of what workers are owed near the back of the line while executives can still collect retention and exit bonuses. This bill would double the amount of unpaid wages employees can claim ahead of other creditors, from $10,000 to $20,000, and remove the 180-day window that now cuts off older claims. It would also prioritize severance, health and pension contributions, and plant-closing penalties; make it much harder for a company to toss out a union contract; require bankruptcy judges to favor buyers who keep jobs and benefits; and cap or claw back executive bonuses when workers or retirees are taking cuts.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees and retirees of companies that file for Chapter 11: they could collect up to $20,000 in unpaid wages ahead of most other creditors with no 180-day cutoff; severance pay, benefit-plan contributions, back pay for labor-law violations, plant-closing penalties, and pension withdrawal liabilities would get higher priority. Retirees' health benefits would be harder to cut, union contracts could be rejected only under a stricter "clear and convincing evidence" standard with a presumption against rejection if executives got bonuses, buyers would have to commit to preserving jobs and benefits to win a court-approved sale, and workers could share in executives' recovered compensation. Unions could also file claims on workers' behalf and keep arbitration going during the case.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees of bankrupt companies

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the priority cap on unpaid wages, salaries, benefits, and commissions from $10,000 to $20,000 and eliminates the requirement that the money was earned within 180 days before the filing, so workers recover more of what they are owed ahead of other creditors.

Gives higher priority in the bankruptcy line to severance pay, contributions to employee benefit plans, back pay and penalties from labor-law violations, WARN Act plant-closing damages, and pension plan withdrawal liabilities.

Restricts executive pay in bankruptcy: insiders, senior executives, top managers, and consultants could only receive payments that are part of a program generally applicable to all full-time employees, retention-pay caps would drop from 10 times to 2 times, bonus caps from 25% to 10%, and a plan's executive pay must be found reasonable compared to similar companies.

Creates a clawback: if a company terminates its pension or wins a court order cutting union or retiree benefits, the estate can recover a proportional share of the compensation paid to directors and top officers in the year before filing, and can claw back transfers made to executives in anticipation of bankruptcy.

Makes it much harder to reject a collective bargaining agreement: the company must pay what it owes under the contract while the case proceeds, propose only the minimum savings essential to exit bankruptcy, and prove its case by clear and convincing evidence — with a presumption against rejection if executives received bonuses during or shortly before the case.

Requires bankruptcy courts to favor, among competing offers, the buyer of a company's assets that preserves jobs, maintains pay and working conditions, and assumes pension and retiree health obligations.

Lets unions file proof of claims on behalf of workers, keeps union grievance and arbitration proceedings alive during the bankruptcy, and requires the company to cover a union's reasonable costs in fighting contract rejection.

Charges unpaid post-filing wages, vacation, severance, and benefit contributions against the collateral of secured lenders, even if the lender had a waiver, so workers get paid from the lender's recovery.

analysis.who_pays: Secured lenders and other creditors who would no longer be first in line for whatever is left of a failed company: unpaid wages up to $20,000, severance, and benefit contributions would come out of the estate and, after filing, from the lender's collateral. Corporate executives, senior managers, department heads, and bankruptcy consultants would lose the retention bonuses, enhanced severance, and exit pay the current system allows, and could be forced to return a share of past compensation when workers or retirees take cuts. Buyers of distressed companies would have to commit to keeping jobs and benefits, limiting cheap asset-stripping. Companies and their lenders could also face more expensive, slower reorganizations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Secured lenders, corporate executives, asset buyers

drawbacks.text: Pushing unpaid wages and benefits onto secured lenders' collateral, and blocking or clawing back executive pay, would reduce what lenders recover in failed companies — which could make credit costlier or scarcer for struggling businesses, or push lenders to force quick liquidations instead of reorganizations.

The stricter standards for rejecting union contracts and the requirement that courts favor buyers who preserve jobs could make some reorganizations harder or more expensive to complete; a company that would have slimmed down and survived under current rules might instead liquidate, costing every job at the firm.
Barring bonuses and outside-pay deals for executives, managers, and consultants could make it harder to retain the people who know the business during a complex restructuring.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a deliberate transfer of recovery in bankruptcies away from secured lenders and executives toward workers, retirees, and pension funds, and its main tools are targeted: a higher wage cap, pay caps benchmarked to other companies, and clawbacks tied to cuts workers and retirees actually suffer. The real risks are economic side effects — costlier credit for distressed firms and harder-to-complete reorganizations — plus a significant added burden on bankruptcy courts, since nearly every pay decision and sale would need individualized findings. The tradeoff favors wage earners; the open question is whether lenders respond by pulling back from distressed companies altogether.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2025 and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has sat since with no hearing or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on April 9, 2025, with five cosponsors: Democrats Schatz, Duckworth, Klobuchar, and Whitehouse, and Republican Josh Hawley.
The Senate read it twice the same day and referred it to the Judiciary Committee; that is the last action on the record.
No hearing, committee vote, or floor vote has been scheduled, and the Congress is still in session, so the bill is technically alive but has not moved.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost — but because the bill has not advanced, the current bankruptcy rules stay in place, which means executives at failing companies keep their bonus and exit-pay options and secured lenders keep first claim on collateral.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Executives and lenders, under status-quo rules

sides.party_line_note: The six sponsors are five Democrats plus one Republican, Josh Hawley, but with no hearing or vote on the record there is no way to know how the full Senate would split.

industries.note: Unpaid wages, vacation, severance, and benefit contributions owed after the filing would be charged against their collateral even over a waiver, and workers' expanded wage claims would jump ahead of them in repayment priority. Their recoveries in failed companies shrink.

Retention bonuses, enhanced severance, and exit pay would be limited to plans that cover all full-time employees and to much tighter caps, and executives could have to return a share of prior compensation when pensions or negotiated benefits are cut.

Consultants are expressly covered by the bonus limits and clawback rules, and transfers to consultants made in anticipation of bankruptcy could be clawed back, cutting into the fees and incentive packages this industry now negotiates out of distressed estates.

industries.industry: Private equity and distressed asset buyers
industries.note: Courts would have to prefer bidders who preserve jobs, pay, and retiree benefits, closing off cheap acquisitions built on shedding workers and obligations; buyers who genuinely keep the business running would still win the assets.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills referred to Senate committee never get a hearing, and this one has sat for months with no committee action. Its one Republican cosponsor gives it a rare bipartisan angle on a labor issue, which could earn it a hearing if Judiciary chooses; without that, its realistic path is dying in committee at the end of this Congress, or surviving only as a provision attached to a larger bill.
